case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal

       competing options already qualifies.

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:

case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.
